canberra.title: A dozen public servants in one agency raking in more than $1 million each
canberra.snippet: A dozen executives working in one public service agency are earning more than a million dollars a year, with one Executive Level 2 (EL2) ...
canberra.content:
Twelve executives working employed by the government’s Future Fund Management Agency are raking in more than a million dollars each annually. Photo: Pressmaster.

A dozen executives working in one public service agency are earning more than a million dollars a year, with one Executive Level 2 (EL2) snaring an annual package of more than $1.5 million.

They all work for Australia’s sovereign wealth fund, the Future Fund Management Agency, and all are generously remunerated with high salaries, bonuses and allowances.

They have direct oversight responsibility for the agency’s $350 billion worth of investments.

The EL2 earning over the $1.5m mark is collecting more than double Prime Minister Anthony Albanese gets, who is on about $622,000 a year base salary (all 12 earn significantly more than the PM).

An EL2 is not even in the APS’s Senior Executive Service (SES), the core leadership group in government administration – department secretaries, deputies and assistant secretaries.

The revelation comes in the recent response to a Greens question that was taken on notice through the Senate process in August.

It has sparked outrage, with the Greens’ finance and public service spokesperson Barbara Pocock saying it raises serious questions about the Federal Government’s economic management and value for money of taxpayer dollars.

“In a cost of living crisis, Australians are hurting. Many would be outraged to learn that a dozen public servants are earning over a million dollars and in some cases double what the Prime Minister earns,” Senator Pocock said.

“We’re not talking about secretaries who run big government departments but employees. How can the government justify this?

“Senior government officials managing large departments with huge budgets and staff would be asking why lower-ranking public servants are getting lottery-sized earnings.

“What kind of public service work warrants a salary of $1 million or 1.5 million dollars? Even the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister don’t earn this much. I think most taxpayers would be questioning whether this represents good value for money.

“The government says it wants to rebuild the public sector, yet it is slashing jobs while paying a handful of public servants millions and outsourcing work to big consultancy firms.

“That’s not how you rebuild the public service. The government is burning up its APS targets.”

In response to the question on notice, Finance and Public Service Minister Katy Gallagher justified the salaries, saying the agency needs to attract highly skilled investment professionals.

“The Future Fund Management Agency participates in highly competitive global markets for talent to identify and access high-quality investment opportunities that deliver strong long-term returns for all Australians,” Senator Gallagher said.

The EL2’s $1,507,170 package includes bonuses and allowance because the executive offers strategic advice to the Future Fund’s board and leads specialist investment teams.

They have “direct oversight and responsibility” for the fund’s investment, the response said.

Because the Future Fund dealt with significant, “at-risk investment outcomes” in commercial markets, a variable pay strategy with bonuses was warranted, she said.

The Minister’s office stressed in the response that the remuneration arrangements comply with Federal Government rules limiting performance bonuses to specific circumstances – and they include roles involving significant investment risks and commercial operations.

The Future Fund manages Australia’s sovereign wealth investments, and the government response to the question on notice also mentioned the fund’s 14.8 per cent return in the 12 months to June 2026 had added $37.4 billion to its portfolio.

The Federal Government is also currently under fire for spending $860 million on external consultants across the APS in the last financial year, including almost doubling what it gave to the scandal-ridden KPMG firm.

KPMG’s taxpayer-funded windfall went from $32 million in 2024-25 to $59 million in 2025-26, with more than 30 contracts worth over $20 million being sealed even after major scandals involving the consultancy giant’s unethical behaviour became public in March this year.

canberra.title: Teen avoids jail for repeatedly raping young woman near house party
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence. A teenager has avoided being sent to jail for the sickening and repeated rape of...
canberra.content:
The now-18-year-old teenager has been handed a suspended sentence for sexual assault. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual violence.

A teenager has avoided being sent to jail for the sickening and repeated rape of a young woman he met at a Canberra house party.

He was 16, nearly 17, when he went to the party in mid-2025 and met the 18-year-old woman, a recently published ACT Supreme Court decision says.

They spoke for a while before he asked her to go for a walk. They left the party, walked to a nearby green belt and began kissing consensually.

But he then got on top of her and forcefully and violently raped her numerous times over about 20 minutes.

At one stage, the woman was crying and said, “Please stop, I don’t want this”, while he assaulted her. He also stopped her from using her phone during his attack.

Afterwards, he pulled her to her feet and they returned to the party.

The now-18-year-old pleaded guilty to a charge of sexual intercourse without consent before he faced the ACT Supreme Court for his sentencing on Tuesday (6 October).

The woman had told the court she asked him to stop, but he refused.

“[She] was excited for adventures and opportunities having just turned 18 years of age, and instead she met with a boy who raped her at a house party which was ‘filled with people [she] knew and went to school with’,” Justice Andrew Muller said.

“She details her loss of dignity, confidence and sense of self because of the assault. [She] can no longer call [her] body [her] own.

“[The] particular circumstances of the offending were humiliating and degrading, involving significant physical force.”

The teen was born in South Asia and moved to Australia to be with his family at the start of 2025.

Justice Muller noted he punched another student at school last year, and he also photographed a fellow student while they were using the toilet.

When asked about the bathroom incident, the now-Year 12 student laughed and said it was a joke.

The teen’s father was also asked about the sexual assault by his son. He said he was “not happy” with it, but his son was “a soft person” who was “never rude or cruel”.

While the teen said he was “sickened” with himself for his actions, he also told the author of a court report the woman was “exaggerating stuff” and he “didn’t force her to do that and this”. He claimed the assault only took place over a matter of minutes.

“[People] might view her differently, I feel sorry for her about that, but that’s about it,” he said.

He said in the future, he will “confirm verbal consent”.

Justice Muller said it was unclear whether the teen was sorry because he realised what he did was wrong, or due to the impact of his charge on his life.

“What is clear is he now realises the giving of consent to sexual interaction necessarily involves clear and active communications to that effect, not just an absence of express refusal,” the judge said.

He took into account the teen’s young age, low risk of reoffending, lack of prior sexual experience, restricted opportunity for social development due to only recently moving to Australia, and the need to promote his rehabilitation.

The teen, who legally cannot be named due to his age, was convicted and sentenced to 18 months’ jail, fully suspended for a good behaviour order.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: ACT Government breached agreement with Ngambri family, court finds
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government has breached the agreement it made with members of a Ngambri family, the Territory’s highest court has found, as...
canberra.content:
Both Ngunnawal and Ngambri people say they have a long connection to the Canberra region. Photo: EPSDD Facebook.

The ACT Government has breached the agreement it made with members of a Ngambri family, the Territory’s highest court has found, as it has not conducted a review into its Indigenous Protocol in a timely manner.

The government has formally recognised the Ngunnawal people as the traditional owners of the land in Canberra for over two decades, even though the Ngambri say they also have a long connection to the region.

In April 2023, the government reached an agreement with members of the House family, who are Ngambri people, to begin a comprehensive review of its Indigenous Protocol.

An interim protocol was put in place for the meantime. This included an acknowledgment of country that, in addition to the Ngunnawal people, recognised “other people or families with connection to the lands of the ACT and region”.

But Paul Girrawah House and Leah Matilda House, two descendants of Elder Henry ‘Black Harry’ Williams, claimed the government did not start the review of its Indigenous Protocol in a reasonable time and launched a civil case to bring about change.

Earlier this month, ACT Supreme Court Justice David Mossop supported their claims in part, finding the government did breach this part of the agreement it made with the family.

He said the government claimed it had no obligation to begin a review of the Indigenous Protocol or of the relevant legislation within 18 months of April 2023, nor by any particular time. The government also claimed it had taken steps to begin the review.

But Justice Mossop said it was uncontroversial that there was an implied term for the obligations in the agreement to be carried out within a reasonable time.

In addition, the terms of the interim protocol made specific reference to a consultation and engagement process “commencing in early 2023”.

“I have concluded that [the government] has not complied with the obligations because it has not carried them out within a reasonable time,” Justice Mossop said.

“The steps necessary to perform the obligation could readily have been commenced within a matter of months of the entry into [the agreement].

“Even allowing for a protracted process, the obligations could have been completed before now.”

The two members of the House family also claimed the government breached their human rights. They claimed the government had signs at the ACT borders and elsewhere that referenced only the Ngunnawal, not the Ngambri, people.

The government admitted certain signs referred only to the Ngunnawal people, but said its electronic signage had been updated to align with the interim protocol.

Justice Mossop rejected the claims of human rights breaches, saying the members of the House family had not been denied their human rights by the government’s actions.

“Given that the evidence does not establish that an unjustified distinction has been drawn between the plaintiffs – as people identifying as Ngambri – and those people identifying as Ngunnawal, no breach of [human rights law] can be established,” he said.

Due to the family’s partial success, the judge adjourned the case to 6 November for the parties to make submissions on the appropriate outcome.

An ACT Government spokesperson said the government acknowledged the findings and recognised the importance of the matters considered in the decision.

“In April 2023 the ACT Government reached a settlement which resulted in an interim change being made to the ACT Government’s Indigenous Protocol and agreement to progress a more fulsome review of the protocol,” they said.

“Such processes take time and need to be community led; however, we acknowledge the finding that this work has not progressed within a reasonable time.

“The government will now carefully review and consider the court’s findings in full ahead of a further hearing in relation to relief following the judgment.”

canberra.title: Tribunal finds ACT Government’s conduct ‘of concern’ in case of allegedly bullied firie
canberra.snippet: The Fair Work Commission deputy president found it likely that an ACT firefighter was “discriminated against” for not being a...
canberra.content:
An ACT firefighter has claimed to the Fair Work Commission that he was bullied and harassed by the United Firefighters Union, and that the ACT Government didn’t follow due dispute resolution processes. Photo: James Coleman.

The Fair Work Commission deputy president found it likely that an ACT firefighter was “discriminated against” for not being a union member and was “subjected to adverse action” by the government after a 2024 incident.

But because of legal technicalities, the firefighter won’t be able to seek recourse from the tribunal and should instead seek compensation through the court system.

In the recently released decision, the firefighter (Applicant) accused United Firefighters Union (UFU) officials of illegally entering the Canberra fire station where he worked, and that he was bullied and intimidated “as the only non-union member on the station”.

He claimed a complaint was made about him to his employer (which is ultimately the ACT Government), and that he was stood down from his duties.

“My employer conducted a flawed Preliminary Assessment (PA), and then formally counselled me in a process that lacked procedural fairness and natural justice … as well as numerous other breaches regarding the process and documentation,” the firefighter submitted to the tribunal.

“I lodged a dispute in relation to the PA process. My dispute went ignored.”

The firefighter disputed the counselling process undertaken by his employer and claimed no consultation had been undertaken regarding the Territory’s agreement with the UFU (which allowed union representatives to enter stations without an entry notice).

“The effect of the above breaches is that my freedom of association … has been trampled, and I am unsafe at work,” he submitted.

“My employment has been injured by these actions in that I have been formally counselled, I am off work on workers’ compensation, and I feel I am being subjected to adverse action. I have no reasonable prospects of returning to such a biased and unsafe workplace that has no regard for the law or the Enterprise Agreement.

“The employer has also misrepresented my rights in the workplace … and I have been bullied by both my employer and the UFU (including employees) for trying to exercise workplace rights.”

The firefighter submitted he’d sought information regarding his concerns through Freedom of Information processes “because the Territory keeps concealing information from me” and the ACT FOI Ombudsman had found Justice and Community Safety Directorate had not
disclosed information that should have been provided.

He escalated his dispute to then-Head of Service Kathy Leigh “after being ignored and persecuted by ACT Fire & Rescue, Emergency Services Agency, and the Justice and Community Safety Directorate”, but claimed no response was sent, breaching another clause.

“The only meeting I have had was the formal counselling meeting, where I was talked over, dismissed, discriminated against, told I would have to watch my back, and had the Territory misrepresent my rights,” the firefighter submitted.

“I feel I have exhausted the options for dispute avoidance at every level in the ACT Government.”

The firefighter claimed the ACT Government failed to take reasonable steps to resolve disputes regarding the preliminary assessment and the formal counselling, and that it falsified documents and failed to maintain records under the Territory Records Act.

He called for individuals and organisations involved to be fined, determinations by the Fair Work Commission, an investigation into the alleged illegal entry and “misrepresentations” by the UFU, consideration of the alleged bullying, harassment and misrepresentations mentioned, full consultation of complaint policies of union reps, and public findings and determinations because “the conduct is unacceptable for registered organisations and government agencies”.

The ACT Government’s legal counsel submitted the first two allegations weren’t covered by the 2024 enterprise agreement, but instead by the 2020 agreement.

It successfully argued this meant the Fair Work Commission had no jurisdiction to make a decision in regard to those disputes.

“In this case, there was no application made to the Commission prior to the 2020 Agreement expiring. There is therefore no jurisdiction for the Commission to exercise,” Fair Work Commission deputy president Lyndall Dean found.

The government also submitted the firefighter hadn’t followed the proper dispute process regarding the third dispute (which related to his escalation of concerns to Ms Leigh and then submitting the Fair Work application 14 days later).

Ms Dean also agreed with this argument.

“Because he has not followed the dispute resolution process, the Commission does not have jurisdiction to deal with the third dispute in the context of this application,” she stated.

Ms Dean said there was nothing to stop the firefighter from “effectively starting [the dispute resolution process] again” and making a further application to the Commission if everything remained unresolved.

The finding also stated the ACT Government had acknowledged the firefighter wasn’t “without remedy”, but it just wasn’t obtainable through the current application.

However, Ms Dean commented the firefighter would have “good prospects of success” if he undertook court actions.

“The conduct of the Respondent in this matter has been of concern. It is evident from a review of the correspondence between the parties that the Respondent pressured Applicant to withdraw this application and told him he would be able to make a new application if discussions between the parties did not resolve the matters in dispute,” she stated.

“It seems as though the Applicant was likely discriminated against because he was not a member of the UFU, was subjected to adverse action, and his place of work became unsafe as a result.”

canberra.title: ‘New city stadium in four years’: Byron pitches directly to PM amid positive reaction to proposal
canberra.snippet: A potentially game-changing proposal for a new all-events 25,000/36,000 seat city stadium has received an enthusiastic response, with the...
canberra.content:
The new city stadium push has attracted powerful backing. From left, Brumbies coach Stephen Larkham, Master Builders ACT CEO Anna Neelagama, Canberra Airport’s Richard Snow and Michael Thomson, Canberra Business Chamber CEO Greg Harford, ACT Property Council executive director Ashlee Berry, Canberra Airport boss Stephen Byron, CDC Data Centres CEO Greg Boorer, Raiders CEO Don Furner Jnr, and AHA ACT branch president Peter Barclay at Wednesday’s launch on City Hill.

A potentially game-changing proposal for a new all-events 25,000/36,000 seat city stadium has received an enthusiastic response, with the business consortium involved hoping to build momentum that could see a facility up and running in as little as four years.

The Canberra Airport-led proposal involves the consortium acquiring the Archbishop’s House site and some of the surrounding carpark next to Commonwealth Park and donating the land to an entity such as a stadium trust.

The Airport group will lend its development expertise to compile a planning package that includes a design, construction costs, and an independent economic and social impact assessment, and present it to the Commonwealth, which would need to approve any proposal and contribute significant funding.

All options are on the table for financing, building and operating the stadium, but it could involve a mix of federal, Territory and private sector involvement. The current arrangement at Canberra Stadium, which the ACT leases from the Commonwealth and is run by the ACT Stadiums Authority, could be replicated, unless a private operator comes forward.

Interestingly, Finance Minister and ACT senator Katy Gallagher was enthusiastic about the proposal, and a social media post is seeking community feedback.

Senator Gallagher’s initial response was: “The opportunity to think about the best use for that site, if the Archbishop land became available, is an opportunity too good to be missed.”

ACT Treasurer and Planning and Sport Minister Chris Steel was more cautious but did not dismiss the idea, which also has the backing of the property industry.

Mr Steel, who was meeting Airport boss Stephen Byron this afternoon (7 October), said the proposal raised the same questions as in previous proposals: event day access, transport, and parking, as well as the technical constraints of the site, including a significant amount of rock, and the fact that it is in an area of national significance.

“It’s very well located next to the new light rail stops at City South … it’s also adjacent to the new Acton Waterfront precinct that will be developed over the coming years, and so it complements both of those things, but there will still need to be work done to address the practical questions,” he said.

Mr Steel indicated that the Commonwealth would need to come to the party because the ACT Government had been clear that its priorities over the next decade included a new Northside Hospital and new schools.

Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton pledged that an ACT Liberal Government would deliver the project, and Liberal Senate candidate Nick Tyrrell was also on board.

“There is a will from the Catholic Church, the Airport group and the Property Council. I would hope we can drag the [ACT] Government kicking and screaming to that position. The [ACT] Government has dropped the ball on what should have been a major city-building project,” he said.

Mr Tyrrell welcomed the Airport’s leadership but said any proposal would still need to stack up on cost to taxpayers, transport and the impact on neighbouring residents.

“Senator Gallagher should meet with the Airport group within the next month and tell Canberrans whether the Commonwealth is prepared to be part of this. Canberrans are tired of the same old studies. They want to see progress,” he said.

At an event with business and sporting leaders this morning, Mr Byron appealed directly to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to back the proposal, saying it would cement his legacy in the national capital.

The favoured design includes an open end for a stage and views to Lake Burley Griffin. Image: Canberra Airport.

Mr Byron said that if government moved quickly to support the idea, a new stadium could be delivered in four years.

“We’re saying four to six months [to deliver the business case], and then we’re going to give the government six to 12 months to make a decision,” he said.

“The quicker they can make that decision, yes or no, the quicker we can get on and build it. The build time is 2.5 years, 30 months, so we could be here in four years’ time when you add all that up, or even less if government can move more quickly and work with us.”

Mr Byron said the design would be modelled on Christchurch’s covered open-ended stadium that would provide a concert stage and views of Lake Burley Griffin at one end.

The consortium includes CDC Data Centres CEO Greg Boorer, who said the stadium could be delivered for less than $500 million, given Christchurch’s cost of $530 million included earthquake proofing.

Mr Boorer said there would also be opportunities for innovative financing including sponsorships, memberships and the sale of corporate boxes.

He said such a stadium would be used far more than the current Bruce facility and have greater potential to generate revenue.

“We think if you can increase the utilisation, the stadium itself will wash its own face, and that’s before you have the knock-on effect of the benefits to all of the businesses around it,” he said.

Canberra Business Chamber CEO Greg Harford said the business chamber was thrilled to support the proposal.

“It’s a world-class stadium to go with a world-class convention centre,” he said.

“We are the nation’s capital. We need to have facilities here in the city that are suitable for that. It will drive substantial economic growth.”

Australian Hotels Association ACT branch president Peter Barclay said it was a wonderful initiative to revitalise the city centre.

Mr Barclay said it would generate a lot of employment, particularly for university students, in the hotels and restaurants that would benefit from a stadium nearby.

Brumbies coach Stephen Larkham said the proposal was a great initiative.

“It’s a great opportunity for both the Brumbies and the Raiders to have a venue that is closer to the centre of town.

“Having played in Christchurch in their stadium over there, the access to the city helps the fans enjoy the experience,” he said

Raiders Don Furner Jnr said the central location would make it easier for fans to travel and would enliven the city.

“You finish work on a Friday night, have a beer, walk across to the football like they do in all cities all around the world,” he said.

“It just brings a vibrancy that you don’t see anywhere else.”

Mr Furner said the location and a new all-weather facility would mean bigger crowds for Raiders and Brumbies games.

Property Council ACT Executive Director Ashlee Berry said Canberra had outgrown its existing facilities and needed a venue capable of attracting major sporting, entertainment and cultural events befitting the nation’s capital.

Ms Berry said major venues should not be viewed simply as sporting infrastructure, but as economic infrastructure that activates city centres, supports local businesses and attracts visitors.

“A world-class stadium would be a city-shaping investment, and the economic benefits would extend well beyond match days,” she said.

With high office vacancy, the CBD needed the kind of boost an all-events stadium would bring, Ms Berry said.

Master Builders ACT CEO Anna Neelagama said switching the site from Bruce to the city would free up land there for much-needed housing, including missing middle and detached homes.

Mr Byron said a social media campaign would launch and the community would be invited to have its say, with businesses also asked to write to the Prime Minister in support.

australia.title: Migration has become a major political talking point – how do parties’ policies compare?
australia.snippet: Labor, the Coalition and One Nation are all planning to reduce net overseas migration – but their plans may not be realistic or beneficia...
australia.content:
The next federal election could be up to two years away, but both major parties – and their biggest threat, One Nation – have already released their immigration policies.

How do they stack up against each other?

How are the major parties proposing to reduce immigration?

Labor has promised to introduce rules to achieve net overseas migration (Nom) of 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 in 2027-28.

In September, the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, announced ministers would be able to prioritise visa applicants with in-demand skills, including in healthcare, construction, education and law enforcement.

Other less critical visa applications are being slowed down to reduce the intake.

Wait times for working holidaymaker visa applications will be stretched to three months to reduce the number entering the country. A ballot system for years two and three with regional work requirements will be introduced.

So-called visa hopping by international students will also be restricted, Burke said, as would visas for family members of students.

The Nom is the overall gain or loss of population through long-term arrivals and departures. It differs from permanent migration, which tracks the annual number of long-term visas offered to skilled workers and family members.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics confirmed in September that Nom had eased to 292,000 in the year to March, from 299,000 in December.

The Nom – a figure notoriously difficult to predict and, until recently, mostly monitored by policy experts and economists – is now being used as a talking point by Labor, the Coalition and One Nation.

This week, the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, announced that the Coalition would more than halve Labor’s Nom forecast, reducing the figure to 100,000 for the first two years from 2028-29.

Taylor rightly noted it was the biggest cut to immigration in Australian history. The Nom target would rise to 130,000 in the third year and 160,000 in 2031-32.

To achieve the drastic reduction, the Coalition would slash bridging and protection visas from more than 400,000 to just 20,000 in four years. Temporary graduate visas, which allow international students to remain in the country for a few months after graduating to find work, will also be cut to 10,000.

What are One Nation and the Greens’ migration policies?

Despite professing to be leading the policy debate on migration, One Nation’s plan lacks detail.

In September, a nine-page document outlined a plan to reduce the number of temporary visa holders by 750,000 if elected to government

Over the three-year period, the minor party said it would impose an annual student visa cap of 115,000, reducing the student visa population to 350,000. It was about 590,000 in 2025-26.

Graduate visas for international students finding work after completing their studies would be capped at 20,000 a year, reducing the visa population to 40,000 over three years. Bridging visas would have a three-year target of 300,000.

After those three years, One Nation said it would set a Nom “ceiling” of 130,000 a year.

The Greens are not supportive of naming a Nom target, saying the “hyper focus” on the figure was the wrong way to deal with immigration levels.

“We are not going to start picking figures out of the air that fall apart at the slightest scrutiny,” the leader, David Shoebridge, said.

“The proof in this is watching how One Nation, the Coalition and Labor have all been chopping and changing their number over the past 18 months as soon as serious scrutiny is applied.”

What do experts say about reducing immigration quickly?

Former senior immigration official Abul Rizvi said before considering the potential consequences of sharply cutting the Nom, it’s worth asking whether any of the parties could actually achieve their target Noms.

Labor has a chance, he said: “If [Labor] maintain that high refusal rate [of visas] together with the changes they’ve announced, they will probably hit the 225 [thousand] target.”

But the Coalition’s proposal appeared near impossible in the current settings, he said. The former bureaucrat claimed the drastic cuts to bridging and temporary graduate visas were unachievable.

The bulk of bridging visas are held by prospective students, partners of Australian citizens, the elderly parents of residents or citizens, and asylum seekers.

“Are you really going to go into an Australian citizen’s home and grab their partner and say, ‘Your bridging visa has been cancelled? Leave the country’. You’re not going to do that,” Rizvi said.

“Firstly, the law won’t let you do that, and secondly, not a good look.”

Rizvi calculated the Coalition could cut Nom to about 200,000, rather than 100,000.

He doubts One Nation could achieve a negative Nom, even by rejecting skilled visa applicants from bringing their partners.

“[One Nation] couldn’t get the negative [Nom] without completely smashing the international education industry, which, on their own figures, they say they don’t intend to do.”

In the event any political party was able to achieve its pledged Nom figure, there would be workforce shortages in the aged care system, he said.

Both Rizvi and Anna Boucher, a University of Sydney immigration expert said the strength of the labour market makes reducing the Nom difficult.

Boucher said the UK and Canada, which have reduced migration numbers in recent years, are now facing serious labour shortages and economic trade-offs in other areas.

Boucher said removing Australian bridging visas could lead to lower migration figures on paper only and an increase in the number of undocumented migrants.

“We have some undocumented overstayers, but it is nothing of the scale of other countries.”

australia.title: Sydney’s ‘king of town hall’ ended up in a pauper’s grave. His support workers are shocked they weren’t told
australia.snippet: Exclusive: The rough sleeper with a ‘massive personality’ now lies buried in a plot with four strangers, despite being well known to loca...
australia.content:
Most homelessness support workers in Sydney knew the “king of town hall”.

The rough sleeper was a familiar presence in the heart of Sydney’s central business district. He’d sit on the town hall steps, offering cheeky advice to passersby and playing music.

The self-proclaimed “king” took a degree of comfort from life in the city centre. He slept beneath the steps, in an alcove near the train station.

He was housed for a period but struggled without the connections he made daily on those steps.

“He was funny, engaging and very well-known across homelessness services in Sydney,” says Jon Swain, an adviser to the Australian Alliance to End Homelessness, who has held senior roles in homelessness coordination in local and state governments.

“He was a massive personality. If you did outreach in Sydney, you knew him.”

Before he died, Swain and other support workers helped the man get into aged care housing support.

But it was what happened next that shocked them.

When the man died this year, the New South Wales government designated him as a “person without means” and took over responsibility for handling his remains.

It then buried him in an unmarked grave at Rookwood cemetery in May, in the same plot as four strangers. Swain had no idea this had happened until he was contacted by the Guardian.

At least 17 other Australians who were clients of Sydney homelessness support services have also been buried in communal unmarked graves by the NSW government, the Guardian can reveal.

The revelation forms part of a three-month investigation that has identified hundreds of unmarked communal graves used to bury disadvantaged Australians.

Using evidence from family and friends, analysis of cemetery registries and aerial and satellite imagery, the Guardian has found that “persons without means” are being buried in bare patches of earth between walkways and old headstones around Rookwood in western Sydney. The vast majority of the graves do not have a plaque or tombstone.

The investigation has prompted an immediate apology from NSW Health, which oversees the process, as well as calls for prime ministerial intervention. The NSW health minister, Ryan Park, has signalled he wants to end the use of unmarked communal graves.

The practice has shocked the homelessness support sector. Major providers like the St Vincent de Paul Society say they were not aware burials were happening in this way.

A homelessness manager at one service, who asked for anonymity, said: “The sector has never been made aware of this practice.

“These people were loved at some point in their lives, they were somebody’s family member or friend. A crowded, yet lonely and desolate end and just like their life on the street these men and women are afforded no privacy in death, and no final resting place of their own.”

The practice is particularly galling to Rev Bill Crews, the head of the Rev Bill Crews Foundation, a support service based in Ashfield.

Crews makes a point of conducting funerals at his own foundation’s expense when he learns that a client or former client has died.

But the Guardian’s investigation has found three individuals buried in the communal graves who were former clients.

Crews says he was never told about the three cases. “They would all have had a dignified funeral and a proper cremation, their ashes would have been scattered,” he says.

Crews has known about the use of unmarked communal graves and has been raising concerns with the NSW government for many years. But he says he has had no response.

“I am so glad now it is coming out. I think nobody believes it, in a way, because it’s not talked about. Nobody believes it, so nobody has pushed for change,” he says.

There are rules for how NSW Health is supposed to manage burials of this kind. It is required to do everything it can to secure funding from family, friends and others for a funeral.

The policy also recommends the agency check with “organisations the deceased may have had an association with while alive”, including charities, to see whether they will help fund a funeral.

Swain says that is not occurring.

He says many people who experience homelessness spend their lives feeling forgotten by the state and as though no one cares about what happens to them. The slow rebuilding of hope in an individual when support is provided is one of the most powerful things a support worker can witness, he says.

“That is why it is so troubling to think that, at the very end of a person’s life, they may have once again been let down,” he says.

“There is something profoundly unsettling about the idea that a person could live through such exclusion and then be buried in a way that seems to further diminish their individuality and humanity one final time.”

Homelessness Australia’s chief executive, Kate Colvin, said governments needs to do much more to prevent premature death and improve healthcare for rough sleepers, but also treat people with dignity and humanity when they die.

That includes by “connecting to the services and community that were in touch with the person who has passed”.

“When someone dies homeless it is often the final indignity in a life marked by poor luck, misfortune or injustice,” Colvin said. “In so many cases, people who die homeless also die early, and their homelessness is a huge contributing factor. To further aggravate this by burying them in an unmarked communal grave should be beneath us as a society. Surely we can do better.”

NSW Health acknowledged that it has not always treated those without financial means with the dignity and respect they deserved, and said it was “committed to changing the way we work”.

The NSW government has signalled greater cooperation with community and charity groups to seek funeral funding.

Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which operates Rookwood, said it has not been funded to provide markings on graves for burials of people without means. A spokesperson said: “There is no evidence to support claims that public burial locations are placed between old headstones, on walkways or in open trenches”.

australia.title: ‘A real-life moment from The Castle’: the retired Australian couple who took on a coal giant and won
australia.snippet: Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan’s four-year fight over MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant coalmine went all the way to the high court Sign up for...
australia.content:
When Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan and a few of their neighbours in the New South Wales Hunter region decided to take on the expansion of a local coalmine, people thought they were “crazy” to engage in the David and Goliath battle.

“When we started this, people thought we were crazy – a little community group taking on a billion-dollar coal company, arguing that the climate harm from burning this coal is our problem too,” Wales says.

The couple live on a farm adjacent to MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant coalmine in Muswellbrook. For more than four years, the retired schoolteachers, former Greens candidates and longstanding environment advocates have been fighting a proposed expansion of the coalmine through the courts, with community members from the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (Dams Heg).

They had a question they wanted a court to answer. Is the state government responsible for the greenhouse gas emissions from the burning of coal after it is sold and exported overseas?

On Wednesday, the high court found that it is.

In a landmark 3-2 ruling, a majority of judges found the Independent Planning Commission of NSW failed to consider imposing conditions aimed at minimising these emissions – known as scope 3 emissions – to the greatest extent possible when it approved MACH Energy’s coalmine expansion.

The approval was ruled invalid.

The case, an appeal by MACH Energy to an earlier decision by the NSW court of appeal, was the first time Australia’s highest court had been asked to consider climate change.

Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

The landmark decision brings to an end a long battle for Wales and her partner, Lonergan.

Wales says when the Mount Pleasant optimisation project was approved in 2022, “if anyone was going to take it on, it was going to be us”.

“Different things pointed us in this direction and we followed them,” Wales says.

When Dams Heg was established 12 years ago, it was because a small number of local professionals – including teachers, a childcare worker and a vet – had shared concerns about the health of the local environment and climate and the effects of mining.

“It really came down to, if not us, who, and if not now, when,” Lonergan says.

“Instead of complaining we needed to take the opportunity to challenge this project.”

In the initial proceedings brought by the community group in the NSW land and environment court, the ruling was in favour of MACH Energy.

Last year, Dams Heg was successful on appeal in the NSW court of appeal, which found the planning commission was required and failed to consider the impacts of all emissions associated with the project on the local environment, including from the exported emissions.

MACH Energy challenged this decision in the high court.

Wednesday’s judgment also found the approval was invalid but on a different basis to the court of appeal, with a majority of judges ruling the planning commission did not consider whether scope 3 emissions could be mitigated.

MACH Energy’s project would have doubled the mine’s coal output to 21m tonnes a year until 2048 and 98% of the projected emissions were scope 3 emissions.

Elaine Johnson, the director of Johnson Legal, which represented Dams Heg, says the decision confirms that Australian governments need to take responsibility for emissions generated by coal exports.

“The court has said that when considering coalmine expansions, our planning authorities must consider how to limit emissions generated from coal burned overseas,” she says.

“Given that Australia is the second largest exporter of coal in the world, this is a very significant judgment. Courts and communities around the world will be looking to what our highest court has said about our responsibilities to reduce emissions from our exports.”

The Climate Council CEO, Amanda McKenzie, likens the win to the storyline from the cult Australian movie The Castle.

“This is a real-life moment from the film The Castle. A community group from the Upper Hunter took on a coal giant, went all the way to the high court, and won,” she says.

The NSW Greens climate change spokesperson and environmental lawyer Sue Higginson says the high court has “exposed the New South Wales coal approval process for the sham it is, and declared that new coal cannot be approved when 98% of the climate pollution are ignored”.

“What an incredible moment in time, that two retired school teachers who have lived and breathed big coal in the Hunter Valley for years and years, Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan have won the day,” she says.

“They are climate heroes and thanks to their incredible advocacy the Hunter community will be spared from the horrific impacts of this proposal.”

She says the decision could also lead to significant legal difficulty for the recently approved Hunter Valley Operations extension – the largest coal project in NSW.

Wales says the community group feels “vindicated” by the court’s decision.

“We’re still a bit disbelieving. But the journey of a thousand miles really begins with the first step,” she says.

“The hardest thing is to overcome your inertia, your self-doubt, your fears, to say there’s a moral compunction here.

“We know it and we can’t turn away from it.”

australia.title: Overseas, Albanese sees ‘the very definition of climate injustice’ – but at home, he still wants coal
australia.snippet: It isn’t hard to see a contradiction between the PM’s message in Fiji and his opposition to legal action to stop a NSW coalmine Get our n...
australia.content:
There are unlikely to be many bigger moments in Australian action on the climate crisis this year than a judgment by the high court on Wednesday.

In what is likely to prove a historic victory, the court sided with community members in the Hunter Valley to strike down a state regulator’s approval of a massive coalmine expansion that could have kept it operating until 2048.

This doesn’t happen every day and the central implication may yet have ramifications for other fossil fuel expansions.

If comments he made in May are taken at face value, the judgment may not please Anthony Albanese. Speaking on 2HD radio in Newcastle, the prime minister said the renewable transition was needed, but the government supported “existing industries” – that is, coal. He hoped the community group would lose as the Mount Pleasant mine expansion had “been through appropriate approvals”.

Well, not according to the high court.

Critics were quick to note the contrast between Albanese’s language opposing legal action to stop a coalmine and the message he delivered over the past three days at a climate conference in Fiji in preparation for the Cop31 summit in Turkey next month.

With Pacific island counterparts, the prime minister helped lead a delegation of about 50 dignitaries to the atoll and reef island nation of Tuvalu. Remote and tiny doesn’t do Tuvalu justice. It is described as the least visited country on the planet. Its land totals just 26 sq km, mostly narrow strips less than 2 metres above sea level. And the distance between the ocean and where most of its people live is getting smaller.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The rate of sea level rise around Tuvalu is about twice the global average, according to Nasa researchers. It means the edges of the nation are being eroded. The delegation was given a presentation illustrating the escalating threat of floods and storm surges washing through homes and infrastructure in the years ahead.

They also saw an example of what the country is doing to give itself the best chance to survive, visiting a land reclamation project on the main atoll of Funafuti that is mostly funded by the Australian government. Sand and gravel dredged from the lagoon is being used to create more than 20 hectares of new, higher ground.

It is a project of hope, and a way to buy time. Possibly the most powerful moment on the quick trip came when the delegation was addressed by a 13-year-old, Melelusi Sokotia, who spoke powerfully about how her friends’ aspirations to be “teachers, doctors, builders” was being overridden by the basic question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.

Melelusi made a plea: “Please work together to protect small islands like ours.”

Later, back in Fiji, a leaders’ plenary heard from the Nepali foreign affairs minister, Shisir Khanal, who travelled for the pre-Cop meeting while his country staggers under the fallout from devastating flooding in August.

While the Pacific confronts a crisis of rising tides and more fierce cyclones, Khanal said Nepal was threatened by melting mountain ice bringing havoc from above. He pointed out the two threats were linked. Melting glaciers ultimately add to rising seas.

The minister said Nepal and the Pacific had something else in common. Neither contributes much at all to the global emissions causing these catastrophes. “Yet our people pay with their lives and development gains for a crisis they had no hand in creating,” he said. “This is the very definition of climate injustice.”

Albanese didn’t ignore this. He took Khanal’s message on enough to repeat part of it – that Nepal faced “extraordinarily traumatic” climate events despite running entirely on hydroelectricity – in a speech before flying out on Wednesday.

He described other examples of extreme events becoming less predictable and more intense as “the science told us would occur”. Climate change wasn’t an abstract future challenge, but “a daily reality that communities are dealing with”. “We saw that first-hand yesterday in Tuvalu,” Albanese said.

The point of Albanese’s speech was to argue for more international investment in the Pacific Resilience Facility, a fund designed to help people in the region cope and live that has received A$100m in Australian government support. He didn’t mention coal.

But when held up against his commentary about the high court judgment, it wasn’t hard to see a screaming internal contradiction – a case of a leader sending conflicting messages to different audiences.

Does Albanese disagree with the high court judgment and still support coal expansion, given its contribution to the crisis he has accurately identified? There was no chance to test this on Wednesday. He left pre-Cop without taking questions from journalists.

None of this is to dismiss the work being done in Fiji. Despite the focus in Australia on the number of leaders who flew to Nadi and Funafuti for the meeting, there is little sense on the ground of it being the failure some have described.

Pre-Cop meetings usually barely make a blip on the public radar. They’re not meant to. They’re a chance for diplomats and bureaucrats to gather before the big end-of-year UN climate summit to lay groundwork and hopefully give it some chance of success.

This year is something else entirely. It is being held in the Pacific in an attempt to bring focus to the plight and needs of its peoples. In that, it has had at least some success. Ministers and their representatives from about 50 governments, including India and European nations, attended. So did thousands of diplomats and civil society members. They talked about Pacific needs.

The trip to Tuvalu included only two national leaders from outside the region – but the EU climate commissioner and the heads of the Asian Development Bank, the Green Climate Fund and the UN climate secretariat were on board. They saw and heard things people doing their jobs should see and hear.

Pacific national and community leaders are not uniform in their views, but they have largely applauded the focus and Australia’s support. Some are also critical, and cynical, about what they see as Australia’s hypocrisy on fossil fuels. That issue isn’t going away.

The ultimate test of this week’s success is whether it helps Cop31 pull off a meaningful agreement on issues to limit climate catastrophe and better direct finance to those that need it to survive, including in the Pacific. To describe that as a challenge in the current geopolitical climate is a spectacular understatement.

One upside of this week has been that the two men responsible for trying to pull that off – the president of the formal negotiations, Australia’s Chris Bowen, and the Turkish Cop31 president, Murat Kurum – have had a few days together to build their relationship and consider how they might do that.

And they have had a consistent and forceful reminder from those around them of why it matters.

  • Adam Morton is Guardian Australia’s climate and environment editor and writes the Clear Air newsletter

world.title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province
world.snippet: Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebo...
world.content:
Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May.

This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment.

A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters.

The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October.

Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August.

Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.

He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, but “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT).

Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”.

He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said.

Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details.

Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi.

After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east.

The response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid.

The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all new Ebola cases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said.

“It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.”

The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said.

Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.”

North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province.

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

world.title: Tigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreads
world.snippet: Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again As renewed fighting has thr...
world.content:
As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia, reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.

Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.

The latest fighting started after months of escalating tensions when the TPLF launched an attack in what it claims was a response to drone strikes by the federal government.

Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian described a broad campaign of forced recruitment in Tigray, targeting men and boys between the ages of 15 and 65.

The Eritrean Defence Forces and Amhara militias, which committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 2020-22 conflict, have switched allegiance and are now fighting in support of the TPLF.

Along with this new alliance, testimonies of forced recruitment, child soldiers and fresh humanitarian crises are emerging out of the already battered region.

Gezu*, 34, who fought with the Tigrayan forces in the 2020-22 war, lost many of his friends on the battlefield and was grateful to survive the deadly conflict. He was planning to start a family when he received a call from the TPLF authorities to join their armed group after the latest outbreak of hostilities.

“I refused to join the war,” he said. “I responded to them to kill me rather than ever force me back to the horrors of the battlefield.

“When they saw no one would join their army willingly, and people fleeing to the capital city, they started rounding up people from the streets. I didn’t want to leave my home town until things started getting worse.”

In the past few months, Tigrayans with the means to leave have been heading for the capital, Addis Ababa, fearing that war was coming. But on 23 September, Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to and from the Tigray region, stranding many people, after Tigrayan forces seized the airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region.

Solomon*, a 52-year-old man who was able to flee to Addis Ababa, said: “The main targets are those between the ages of 15 and 40. I have seen the armed group of the TPLF rounding up people as young as 15 and 16 at gunpoint from the streets and public transportation areas.

“I know parents who tried to save their children by showing medical certificates. The officers don’t care whatever internal disease you have; they forcefully recruit anyone whose hands, eyes and feet work.”

Ephrem, 40, is a father of three who, fearing conscription, was planning to leave the region weeks before the fresh fighting erupted. “Every time I go outside the house, my wife and the kids are anxious. The kids cry fearing that I will be rounded up from the street.

“People who have money protect themselves and their children from the forced recruitment by bribing the officers. It is devastating; no one wants to join the war,” he said.

The Tigray region has been under siege for the past week, when citizens’ bank accounts were abruptly frozen by the federal government, leaving people unable to withdraw their money. The banks have since reopened with a daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr (£9) and with long queues forming outside.

Negus*, an elderly man in Mekelle, said: “We don’t know for how long the siege and the war are going to stay. A daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr can hardly afford to buy the skyrocketing food prices. It is impossible to leave this embattled region. There is no way for relatives outside to send medicine or cash. I am just hoping it all ends soon.”

Internet and phone communications were also cut off on the orders of the TPLF until this week, leaving families desperate for news of relatives in the region.

Meanwhile, the Ethiopian government has been accused of carrying out indiscriminate drone airstrikes and there have been reports of attacks by the opposition forces coming close to Addis Ababa.

An estimated 300,000 to 800,000 civilians died during the Tigray conflict, according to the British government. The Ethiopian army, Eritrean forces and Amhara nationalist “fano” militias, have previously committed grave atrocities against the Tigrayan population that amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia. Tigrayan forces were also accused in an Amnesty report of committing atrocities during the war.

* Names have been changed to protect their identities

world.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
world.snippet: After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underw...
world.content:
On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.

Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.

Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.

Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.

After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.

Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.

“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.

“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”

On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.

“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”

Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.

When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”

The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.

In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.

“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”

With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.

She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.

“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

world.title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed
world.snippet: Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory Court officials and craftspeopl...
world.content:
Court officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.

The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.

Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.

Writing in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.”

The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.

But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.

Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.

“This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century,” Campbell told the Guardian, but she said this was the first study to look at trauma and cause of death while examining human remains from the tombs.

Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye.

Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.

The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler.

“For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.”

Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty.

Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”.

She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.”

Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant.

“If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said.

world.title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
world.snippet: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown An Egyptian journalist has...
world.content:
An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.

Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.

On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.

Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.

Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.

“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”

The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.

Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.

The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.

More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.

The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.

The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing.

This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters.

While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”

Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.

Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.

Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsadaash are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.
